pos: n. (the head of a family of the Nethinims who returned from Babylon; also, as Reaia, a Reubenite in the line of Joel)
etymology: Hebrew Re'ayah, the LORD hath seen, from ra'ah, to see, with Yah; named at Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:50, and as Reaia at 1 Chronicles 5:5.
biblical_def: Reaiah is the head of a Nethinim household in the roll of the return: “The children of Giddel, the children of Gahar, the children of Reaiah” (Ezra 2:47), repeated in Nehemiah's copy of the same register (Nehemiah 7:50). The Nethinims were the given ones, the temple servants who drew water and cut wood for the house of God, and their households are listed name by name alongside the priests and the Levites. The Authorized Version spells the name Reaia of a different man, a Reubenite: “Micah his son, Reaia his son, Baal his son” (1 Chronicles 5:5), in the descent of Joel whose house was carried away by Tilgath-pilneser. A third man of this name, the son of Shobal in Judah (1 Chronicles 4:2), is the same person the Chronicler elsewhere calls Haroeh, the seer, and he has his own entry under that headword. The meaning is a confession: the LORD hath seen. It is the claim Hagar made in the wilderness when she called the LORD Thou God seest me.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Reaiah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the LORD hath seen; head of a family of the Nethinims, Ezra 2:47, and (as Reaia) a Reubenite, 1 Chronicles 5:5.
webster_full: Hebrew Re'ayah, the LORD hath seen, or whom Jehovah regards.
From ra'ah, to see or to look upon, compounded with Yah.
It occurs at Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:50 of a family of the Nethinims.
The form Reaia stands at 1 Chronicles 5:5, of a Reubenite in the line of Joel.
The Judahite son of Shobal who bears this name at 1 Chronicles 4:2 is the Haroeh of 1 Chronicles 2:52, and is treated under that headword.

corruption_summary: Being seen is now a social good to be sought and granted; the Hebrew name says that God sees, which is comfort and warning at once.
corruption_paragraphs: To be seen has become a thing people ask of one another, and failing to see someone is counted a wrong. The biblical confession is different in object and in effect. It is not that others see me but that God does — which comforted a runaway slave girl in the desert and terrified a king on his roof. “And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me” (Genesis 16:13).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the omniscience of God as a settled fact of daily life, not a doctrine kept in a cupboard. The Nethinim household that bore this name came back from Babylon to cut wood and draw water for the temple, unseen by everyone except the One the name confesses.
roots_summary: Hebrew Re'ayah, the LORD hath seen; a Nethinim family, Ezra 2:47; as Reaia, a Reubenite, 1 Chronicles 5:5.

The Judahite of this name at 1 Chronicles 4:2 is the Haroeh of 1 Chronicles 2:52.
